kingdom_identity_not_by_colour_alone.evidence: Set D's crimson keep has a multi-spire cluster of tall cone roofs, while the emerald keep has a hipped/pyramid roof with a flat stepped crown, and the watchtower is a stacked spire versus a pyramid roof. These are clearly different shapes at 170 studs. Set C's keep also differs (cones vs a hipped roof) and its tower differs (spire vs dome), so it is close behind, but it is less legible at distance and the emerald keep looks like a different building type. Set A uses the identical silhouette in both hues: the keep differs only in roof colour, and the watchtower differs only slightly in roof colour and shape (pyramid vs a similar pyramid). Set A therefore fails D-033.

hybrid_pick.why: D's primitive buildings carry the kingdom silhouettes and cost the least among the sets that pass on silhouette. C's soft, rounded trees are the best look, but they cost about 30k triangles. B's wheat is the most readable and cheapest. Mixing D buildings with C trees and B wheat gives a coherent faceted look, but C's textured, rounded trees and A/C's detailed meshes sit beside D's flat blocky shapes, so the style would not be fully uniform. Part count is a concern for D: about 900 Parts for one settlement, and four kingdoms would be heavy.

A: Keep and watchtower silhouettes are the same in both hues; only the colour of the roof differs, which violates D-033.
Trees are one repeated cone shape with little variation; the stand reads as a single dark green mass with no oak/deciduous contrast.
The L1 keep is a tall narrow tower with no wide footprint, so it reads as a watchtower at 170 studs. The level 3 keep is also small compared with its 46-stud footprint.
B: Wheat only: uniform rows of identical yellow cones, with no variation between plots and no fence or border detail.
The flat, tilted slab shape reads as a roof rather than a field at 82 studs.
Only wheat is covered, so B cannot be judged as a building or tree set.
C: Triangle cost is very high: keep 13.5k, settlement 68k, trees 29k. It cannot be afforded across four kingdoms plus hundreds of trees.

The emerald keep looks like a different building from the crimson one (flat roofs versus cone towers), which is good for D-033 but reads as inconsistent; the keep and house are also dull and brownish and fade into the grass at 170 studs.
The wheat is thin, with small beds and faint colour at 170 studs; the thatch house is similar in colour to the grass.
D: Roughly 900 Parts per settlement (a keep alone is 218) is a heavy draw-call and physics load across four kingdoms.
Wheat is just flat tan slabs (17 Parts), which look like wooden planks or a roof rather than a crop; the construction stages are bare scaffolding that is hard to read.
The 82-stud house and barracks are tall, flat, boxy slabs with a large red roof; proportions beside the citizens look oversized and less refined than A/C.

notes: No single set wins every family. D is the best for D-033 and for readability at 170 studs, but its Part count is a problem and its house and barracks look boxy. A is cheap and cohesive, but it fails the kingdom-identity rule because its hues share silhouettes, and its trees lack variety. C looks best close up, but its triangle cost is prohibitive. B's wheat is the clear pick. Mixing sets is only partly one style, so the buildings and trees need more work before launch, and none of the evidence here is a Studio play test.
